label: section_header
content: 1. Executive Summary

label: text
content: Residential solar has moved from a niche technology to a mainstream household investment. Between 2015 and 2025 the installed cost of a home system fell from USD 3.80 per watt to USD 1.50 per watt, a reduction of about 60 percent. Over the same period global residential capacity grew from 38 GW in 2018 to 166 GW in 2025, more than quadrupling in seven years.

label: text
content: Asia-Pacific holds the largest share of residential capacity at 42 percent, followed by Europe at 27 percent and North America at 18 percent. Payback periods vary widely: the Middle East and Africa average 4.9 years, while North America averages 8.6 years because of lower electricity prices and higher labor costs.

label: text
content: The main technology trend is a shift from polycrystalline panels to monocrystalline PERC and TOPCon modules. Heterojunction (HJT) panels reach the highest efficiency at 24.0 percent and the longest lifespan at 35 years, but cost USD 0.38 per watt compared with USD 0.22 per watt for polycrystalline panels.

label: section_header
content: Key findings

label: text
content: (1) A typical 6 kW system costs USD 9,000 installed. (2) Panels account for 38 percent of that cost and installation labor for 22 percent. (3) A 5 kW system in a temperate climate produces about 7,500 kWh per year and avoids 3,375 kg of CO 2 . (4) Output peaks in June at 880 kWh for the reference 5 kW system.

label: section_header
content: 2. Introduction

label: text
content: Solar photovoltaic (PV) modules convert sunlight directly into electricity using semiconductor cells. When photons strike a cell, they free electrons and create a current of direct current (DC) electricity. An inverter then converts the DC output into alternating current (AC) suitable for household appliances and the utility grid.

label: text
content: This report reviews the technology options available to homeowners, the economics of installation, global adoption trends, environmental benefits, and practical maintenance. It is organized so that each section contains a mix of narrative text, tables, charts and diagrams, which makes it suitable for evaluating document-understanding systems.

label: text
content: The scope is limited to grid-tied residential systems between 3 kW and 10 kW. Utility-scale plants, off-grid cabins and commercial rooftops are outside the scope. Where the report quotes a figure, it is the reference value used throughout the document so that questions can be checked against a single consistent source.

label: section_header
content: 3. Solar Panel Technology

label: text
content: Five panel technologies dominate the residential market. Their main differences are conversion efficiency, cost per watt, expected lifespan, and annual degradation, which is the percentage of output lost each year. Table 1 compares them.

Table 1: Comparison of residential solar panel technologies

| Technology             |   Efficiency (%) |   Cost (USD/W) |   Lifespan (years) |   Degradation (%/yr) |
|------------------------|------------------|----------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| Monocrystalline PERC   |             21.5 |           0.28 |                 30 |                 0.45 |
| Monocrystalline TOPCon |             23.0 |           0.31 |                 30 |                 0.40 |
| Polycrystalline        |             17.0 |           0.22 |                 25 |                 0.70 |
| Thin-film (CdTe)       |             18.5 |           0.25 |                 25 |                 0.50 |
| Heterojunction (HJT)   |             24.0 |           0.38 |                 35 |                 0.25 |

label: caption
content: Table 1: Comparison of residential solar panel technologies

label: text
content: Monocrystalline PERC (Passivated Emitter and Rear Cell) panels remain the volume leader, with an efficiency of 21.5 percent and a degradation rate of 0.45 percent per year. TOPCon (Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact) improves on PERC by raising efficiency to 23.0 percent and lowering degradation to 0.40 percent per year for a modest price premium of USD 0.03 per watt.

label: section_header
content: 3.1 Why efficiency matters

label: text
content: Efficiency determines how much power a panel produces per square meter. On a small roof, a higher efficiency panel can be the difference between meeting a household's demand and falling short. A 24.0 percent HJT module produces about 12 percent more energy per square meter than a 21.5 percent PERC module, so it can justify its higher price on space-constrained roofs.

label: section_header
content: 3.2 Thin-film and polycrystalline panels

label: text
content: Polycrystalline panels are cheaper but less efficient at 17.0 percent, and they degrade faster at 0.70 percent per year. Thin-film cadmium telluride (CdTe) modules reach 18.5 percent and perform comparatively well in high heat and diffuse light, but their lower efficiency makes them uncommon on homes.

label: section_header
content: 4. Economics of Residential Solar

label: text
content: The most important economic trend of the decade is the steady decline in installed cost. Figure 1 shows the fall from USD 3.80 per watt in 2015 to USD 1.50 per watt in 2025. The steepest single-year drop was between 2015 and 2016, when the cost fell by USD 0.40 per watt, while the most recent drop, 2024 to 2025, was USD 0.15 per watt.

label: text
content: Year

label: text
content: Hardware prices fell faster than installation costs. Panel prices dropped by roughly 70 percent over the decade, but labor, permitting and customer acquisition costs fell much more slowly, which is why labor is now the second largest cost item.

label: text
content: Global residential capacity grew every year between 2018 and 2025. Figure 2 shows that capacity rose from 38 GW in 2018 to 46 GW in 2019, 58 GW in 2020, 72 GW in 2021, 90 GW in 2022, 112 GW in 2023, 138 GW in 2024 and 166 GW in 2025. The largest absolute increase was between 2024 and 2025 at 28 GW, ahead of 26 GW between 2023 and 2024.

content: 6. Performance and Roof Area

label: text
content: Annual generation scales almost linearly with usable roof area. In a sample of 60 homes, the correlation coefficient between roof area and annual generation was r = 0.99. As a rule of thumb, each square meter of usable roof produces about 165 kWh per year in the study climate.

label: section_header
content: 7. Environmental Impact

label: text
content: Each kilowatt-hour generated by a home system displaces grid electricity. Using a grid emission factor of 0.45 kg of CO 2 per kWh, Table 4 estimates the annual emissions avoided for three common system sizes. One tree is assumed to absorb about 21.8 kg of CO 2 per year.

label: caption
content: Table 4: Annual CO2 avoided by system size

label: text
content: The carbon payback time of a modern panel, which is the time needed to offset the emissions from manufacturing it, is between one and two years. Over a 30 year lifespan, a panel therefore generates clean electricity for more than 90 percent of its life.

label: section_header
content: 8. Operation, Maintenance and Safety

label: text
content: Residential systems have no moving parts and need little maintenance. Panels should be inspected visually twice per year, and cleaned when dust, pollen or bird droppings visibly reduce output. In rainy climates natural rainfall usually keeps panels clean enough.

label: section_header
content: 8.1 Common inverter fault codes

Table 5: Inverter fault codes, causes and recommended actions

| Code   | Description        | Likely cause                            | Action                                     |
|--------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| E01    | Grid overvoltage   | Utility voltage above 253 V             | Wait 5 min; call utility if it persists    |
| E02    | Ground fault       | Damaged cable insulation or moisture    | Shut down; inspect by licensed electrician |
| E03    | Over-temperature   | Blocked inverter vents                  | Clear ventilation; check ambient heat      |
| E04    | DC arc fault       | Loose connector or damaged panel wiring | Shut down immediately; professional repair |
| E05    | Communication loss | Wi-Fi drop or faulty gateway            | Restart gateway; check router signal       |

label: caption
content: Table 5: Inverter fault codes, causes and recommended actions

label: section_header
content: 9. Conclusions

label: text
content: Residential solar is now cost-competitive in most regions. The combination of falling hardware prices, improving panel efficiency and growing policy support suggests that capacity will keep growing, although labor and permitting costs are now the main barrier to further price reductions.

label: text
content: For homeowners the key decision factors are roof area, local electricity price, available incentives and panel technology. For policymakers, the priorities are simplifying permitting and supporting grid upgrades that can absorb distributed generation.
